name: Bill Clinton
summary: Clinton is a centrist Democrat associated with the 'New Democrat' and Third Way approach. He combined fiscal discipline, free trade, welfare-to-work and tough-on-crime policies with support for health coverage, a higher minimum wage, affirmative action, abortion rights, gun limits and climate agreements. He used force for humanitarian ends through NATO, and later in life reversed his positions on DOMA and parts of the 1994 crime bill.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Proposed the 1993 Health Security Act, under which every American would get a health security card guaranteeing a comprehensive benefit package, financed mainly through employer-based private insurance. Said in 2000 he wanted quality, affordable care for all. Not single-payer, but a state-backed guarantee of coverage.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Asked Congress in 1995, 1996, 1998, 1999 and 2000 to raise the minimum wage, from $4.25 and then by a dollar over two years; he argued that a modest increase does not cost jobs. A rise of about a dollar is a meaningful but not 'substantial' step, hence +1.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Mixed: said 'the era of big Government is over' and championed free enterprise and open markets, but also insisted citizens cannot be left to fend for themselves and that government invests in education and health; he did not say markets allocate better than government.

public-ownership.rationale: No recorded position found in the sources reviewed.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Signed the 1993 budget that raised income taxes on the wealthiest Americans; in 1992 asked those earning over $200,000 to pay their 'fair share'; in 2012 attacked tax cuts weighted to upper incomes.

reviewHistory.rationale: Mixed record: signed deregulatory laws (Telecommunications Act 1996, Gramm-Leach-Bliley 1999, Commodity Futures Modernization Act), yet asked for a Patients' Bill of Rights against HMOs, campaign finance limits and tougher health and children's protections.

limit-guns.rationale: Signed the Brady Act in 1993 and the 1994 crime bill that banned assault weapons and juvenile handgun ownership; these are significant limits on gun ownership, short of strict ones.

reviewHistory.rationale: Signed the Brady Act and the 1994 assault weapons ban, vowed in 1995 not to let the ban be repealed, and asked for restored waiting periods, juvenile gun bans and 'commonsense gun safety legislation'. These are significant limits but not strict limits on gun ownership.

free-trade.rationale: Signed NAFTA, led the China-WTO agreement and boasted of 240 trade agreements; said the US must 'shape this global economy, not shrink from it'.

nation-first.rationale: Said the US must 'shape this global economy, not shrink from it' and that no free nation can enjoy security in isolation; argued for partnerships, NATO and the UN.

open-borders.rationale: Increased border controls by 50 percent, hired record numbers of border agents and signed an order against federal contracts to firms hiring illegal immigrants; said 'we are also a nation of laws'.

limit-growth.rationale: Said the US has always found a way to 'clean the environment and grow the economy at the same time'.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Nulled (later pass): the Kyoto Protocol was signed for the United States by the acting UN ambassador, with the statement that it would not go to the Senate without developing-country participation; that record points both ways on drastic action.

reviewHistory.rationale: Signed the Kyoto Protocol in 1998 and called global warming the greatest environmental challenge of the new century, proposing tax incentives and clean-energy investment and promoting fuel-economy rules; the measures proposed were more moderate than 'drastic'.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Said the old welfare system undermined the values of work and family and should be a 'second chance, not a way of life'; signed the 1996 law ending the open-ended entitlement. But he also expanded child care and the EITC, and opposed deep cuts, so the evidence is mixed. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: In the 1994 State of the Union he called for resolving "to promote democracy abroad" and named support for the advance of democracy elsewhere the best strategy for security and peace.

pay-off-national-debt.rationale: In the 2000 State of the Union he said the country could pay down the national debt entirely in 13 years and be debt-free for the first time since 1835, and asked Congress to stay the course.

notes: Recent positions govern where he changed: he signed DOMA (1996) but supported same-sex marriage by 2009 and urged DOMA's repeal in 2013; he said in 2015 that the 1994 crime bill's incarceration provisions had overshot. Many answers rest on his presidential speeches (1992-2000) and signed laws; positions he stated only as president may differ from his private views. Items without a quoted or recorded position (e.g. unions, encryption, surveillance, central bank independence, Glass-Steagall as a personal view) are left null. DADT, the 1999 Glass-Steagall repeal and the 1996 Telecommunications Act were signed or accepted under congressional pressure, so they are cited only where a statement matches. Later pass (2026-11-12, rules 7): read all 39 Miller Center speeches and the Gutenberg State of the Union and inaugural texts, searched them by keyword for the statement themes (democracy abroad, international courts, genocide, taxes, crime, guns, privatization, immigration, unions, nuclear weapons and power, campaign finance, military service of gay people), and replaced encyclopedia-based record answers with signing statements and official releases. Themes with no stated position of his in those texts (unions, privatization of pensions, surveillance, encryption, schooling beyond vouchers and charters) stay null.
